passage:
Last spring I sat on my first hiring panel. I'm Uma, the youngest woman on it, and I was nervous about getting it wrong. One candidate, Pankaj, had grown up three streets from my school in Coimbatore. We laughed about the same bakery. I liked him instantly, and that was exactly what worried me.
Before the interviews I had written four things on a card: problem-solving, clarity, teamwork, willingness to learn. After Pankaj left, I scored him against the card, not against the bakery. Then I asked myself: if he had come from a town I'd never heard of, would I give him the same marks? Honestly, one mark lower.
I also asked the team to add two candidates from colleges we never visit. One of them, a quiet woman from Silchar, got the job.

qa.q: What four things did Uma write on her card?
qa.a: Problem-solving, clarity, teamwork and willingness to learn.

qa.q: Why did liking Pankaj instantly worry Uma?
qa.a: She knew the shared bakery and hometown could make her rate him higher than his answers deserved, and she wanted to be fair. 🤔

qa.q: What choice did Uma make after scoring Pankaj, and how did it change the result?
qa.a: She asked whether she'd give the same marks to someone from an unfamiliar town, dropped his score by one, and pushed for candidates from unvisited colleges, one of whom got the job.

qa.q: How might the woman from Silchar see this hiring if Uma hadn't pushed for new colleges?
qa.a: She might never have been interviewed at all, and would likely have assumed the company simply wasn't open to people like her.

grounding: A young woman on a hiring panel uses a criteria card, seeks candidates unlike herself and tests her call against her hometown pull.

passage:
Supervisor's notes, Friday
Minakshi had to pick one person from her team for the client visit to Pune. Her closest colleague, Bhavna, went to the same college and joined the same week; they eat lunch together daily. Everyone assumed Bhavna would go.
Instead, Minakshi wrote down the three things the client needs: product knowledge, calm under questions, Marathi. She asked me to add Rafiq from the night shift, whom she barely knows, to the list. She told me later, "If Rafiq were my friend and Bhavna a stranger, who would I send?" Rafiq scored higher on two of three.
She told Bhavna herself before the list went out, with the reasons. Bhavna looked hurt for a minute, then asked what to work on for the next visit.
Plan: I'll use Minakshi's list format for all team picks this quarter.
— Harish, supervisor

qa.q: Where was the client visit?
qa.a: The client visit was to Pune.

qa.q: Why might Minakshi have asked herself who she would send if Rafiq were her friend?
qa.a: She was wary that her friendship with Bhavna could quietly tilt her choice, and swapping the two in her mind was a way to catch that pull.

qa.q: What choice did Minakshi make before the list went out, and why did it help?
qa.a: She told Bhavna herself, with the reasons, so the decision felt honest rather than like a betrayal, and Bhavna turned it into a plan for next time.

qa.q: How might Rafiq, on the night shift, see being picked for the visit?
qa.a: Rafiq may feel noticed for real skills, since people on the night shift are easy for the day team to overlook.

grounding: A supervisor records a young colleague choosing by stated criteria, adding someone outside her circle and swapping friend and stranger in her head.

12 March, late
Big call today: whose façade design goes to the client. Two finalists. Sayan's, from our little Bengali corner of the office, where we joke in Bangla over tea. And Francis's, who joined from Kochi and mostly eats at his desk.
My gut said Sayan straight away. So I did what I'd promised myself: wrote the brief's three needs on a sticky note (daylight, cost, local material) and marked both designs with the names covered. Francis won two of three.
Then the harder test: if Francis were one of our tea group, would I hesitate at all? No. That settled it.
Tomorrow I'll also ask Francis to lunch. I realised I've never once asked him.
Ma called tonight and I told her about it. She said, "Good girl. Fair is fair." 🙂
— Ankita

qa.q: What three needs did Ankita write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Daylight, cost and local material.

qa.q: Why did Ankita cover the names before marking?
qa.a: Ankita felt uneasy that her gut already leaned toward Sayan from the tea group, and she wanted the designs judged without that pull.

qa.q: What small choice at the end of the day could help Ankita beyond this one decision?
qa.a: Asking Francis to lunch starts to widen her circle, so the next close call isn't shaped only by who she already knows.

qa.q: What might it be like for Francis to eat at his desk while others joke in Bangla over tea?
qa.a: Francis may feel outside the office's warm corners, so being judged on the work itself, and then invited to lunch, could matter a lot.

grounding: A young architect uses blind criteria, reaches out to a colleague unlike her and asks if she'd decide the same for her own group.

passage:
At the block development office in a kasba near Dhule, Gargi, twenty-five, had to choose ten farmers for a free drip-irrigation training. By noon, most names on her list came from her own village and the one next to it; people she knew, who had phoned her directly.
She looked at the list and felt uneasy. Were these really the best choices, or just the familiar ones?
She wrote three rules on a sheet: small landholding, a water problem, and nobody from the same family twice. Then she asked Harsha, the field assistant, "Can you bring me names from the villages across the river? I don't know anyone there."
Harsha came back with fourteen names. Gargi scored everyone using the same sheet. Four from her village stayed on the list. Six new names joined it.
One of them, an old woman, came to the office just to see the list, and touched it twice.

qa.q: How many new names joined Gargi's list after she used the sheet?
qa.a: Six new names joined it.

qa.q: What was Gargi worried about when she looked at her first list?
qa.a: She worried that the names were chosen because they were familiar, people from her own and the next village who had phoned her, not because they were the best choices.

qa.q: Which steps did Gargi take to make the selection fairer?
qa.a: She wrote three clear rules, asked Harsha to bring names from villages across the river where she knew no one, and scored everyone on the same sheet.

qa.q: What might the old woman's touching the list twice suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she could hardly believe she was included, and perhaps that people like her had often been left out of such lists before.

grounding: It shows a young officer using clear criteria and reaching out to people unlike herself, checking she would make the same call regardless of group.

passage: Nadia was shortlisting volunteers for the youth centre in Madrid, and two files sat side by side. Laura had gone to Nadia's own university, played in the same orchestra, and wrote an application that felt like a letter from a friend. Pablo had grown up in a small town in the south, left school at sixteen and later finished his diploma at night. Nadia caught herself smiling at Laura's file and frowning at Pablo's spelling. She stopped. She took out her criteria sheet: experience with teenagers, reliability, languages. Pablo had coached a football team for five years and spoke three languages. Laura had tutored once. Then she asked herself: if Pablo had gone to my university, would I be hesitating? She wouldn't. She put both on the interview list, Pablo first.

qa.q: How long had Pablo coached a football team?
qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: What made Nadia stop herself?
qa.a: She caught herself feeling warm toward Laura and doubtful about Pablo for reasons unrelated to the job, and felt uneasy about it.

qa.q: What steps did Nadia use to make a fair call?
qa.a: She used her criteria sheet and asked whether she would hesitate if Pablo had gone to her own university.

qa.q: What might reaching the interview mean for Pablo?
qa.a: It gives him a fair chance based on his real experience, not on shared background with the reviewer.

passage:
Dear Pema,
Before Friday's scholarship meeting, I want to share something I noticed in myself, in case it's useful.
When I read the forty applications last week, I ranked the Pune students higher on "potential" without really knowing why. Then I realised: I'm from Pune. Their essays mentioned places and teachers I know, and it felt like they were my people.
So I re-read all forty using only our three written criteria: marks, need and community work. For each Pune student I also asked: would I give the same score if this student were from Latur or Kohima? Four scores went down. Two students from the northeast went up.
Could we both try this check before Friday? And maybe invite someone from outside our city onto the panel next year?
Warmly,
Pallavi

qa.q: What were the three written criteria?
qa.a: Marks, need and community work.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel on noticing the Pune students ranked higher?
qa.a: Pallavi felt uneasy on realising the essays felt like Pallavi's own people, which had quietly lifted their scores.

qa.q: What check did Pallavi use, and why does it make the choice fairer?
qa.a: Scoring only on the three criteria and asking whether a Pune student would get the same score if from Latur or Kohima, which cancels the pull of the home group.

qa.q: How might Pema react to the letter?
qa.a: Pema might feel appreciative of Pallavi's honesty and willing to try the same check before Friday.

grounding: A young panellist writes about re-scoring applications on clear criteria and checking whether home-town students got an unfair lift.

passage: Thanks for having me, Ira. So, I'm Gurleen, and last year I hired for my team for the first time. And the first thing I noticed? I liked every candidate from my own college. Same jokes, same professors, I felt at home in five minutes. That scared me a little. So I made three rules for myself. One: write down the criteria before reading any CV. Two: make sure the shortlist had people who didn't look or sound like me. I asked a colleague from a different city to find two extra candidates. Three: before every decision, I asked myself, "Would I say the same if this person was from my college?" One candidate from a small-town college, very quiet, scored highest on the actual tasks. My gut wanted the other one. I hired the quiet one. She's our best analyst now.

qa.q: How many rules did Gurleen make for hiring?
qa.a: Three rules.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling on liking every candidate from the same college?
qa.a: Gurleen felt a little scared, worried that comfort with familiar people was steering her choices.

qa.q: Which of Gurleen's rules seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Asking "Would I say the same if this person was from my college?" before each decision, because it tests the call directly for in-group bias.

qa.q: How might the quiet candidate from the small-town college have been affected without these rules?
qa.a: She might have lost the job to a more familiar candidate, despite scoring highest on the actual tasks.

grounding: Shows a young professional using clear criteria, seeking candidates unlike Gurleen, and checking each call against own-group bias.

passage: I was taking notes at the planning meeting when Chetan read out his list of speakers for the conference. Six names. I knew at least four; they were his batchmates. Bhavna listened, nodded, and then did something I'd never seen a chair do. She asked everyone to write the selection criteria on the whiteboard first: expertise, fresh ideas, a mix of regions, a new voice. Then she put Chetan's six beside the criteria. Two fitted well. Four were friends of friends. She didn't say that. She just asked, "Who's missing?" Someone mentioned a researcher from Guwahati. Someone else, a woman who ran a rural lab. Bhavna added them. Then she said, "Let's check: would we pick these same people if none of us knew them?" Chetan went red, but he nodded. The final list kept two of his names.

qa.q: How many speakers were on Chetan's list?
qa.a: Six names.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt when he went red?
qa.a: Chetan probably felt embarrassed, seeing that most of his picks were friends rather than the best fits for the criteria.

qa.q: What made Bhavna's approach fair?

qa.q: Why did Bhavna ask "Who's missing?" instead of criticising Chetan's list?
qa.a: She seemed calm and fair-minded, wanting to widen the list without shaming Chetan in front of everyone.

Shalini, sit, the chai will get cold. You asked how I choose people for my team. Let me tell you about my first hiring panel.
I was new, and the first candidate was from my own college. Same hostel, same professors, even the same canteen jokes. I liked him before he opened his mouth. The next one came from a small polytechnic, spoke slowly, no fancy words. My gut said: the first one.
So I did something that felt strange then. I took out the sheet we had agreed on before the interviews, three points for the design task, two for explaining it, one for teamwork, and scored both again with the names covered. The polytechnic boy's design was better. Then I asked myself, if he were from my hostel, would I hesitate? No. So I didn't.
After that, I, Damini, started asking for CVs from colleges I had never heard of. That polytechnic boy has run our workshop for twenty years now.

qa.q: What were the three parts of the scoring sheet?
qa.a: The sheet gave three points for the design task, two for explaining it and one for teamwork.

qa.q: Why did Damini feel drawn to the first candidate?
qa.a: Damini felt a warm, easy familiarity because of the shared college, hostel and canteen jokes, so liking him felt like good judgement at the time.

qa.q: Which choice during the panel turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Rescoring both on the agreed sheet with names covered, and asking whether the polytechnic candidate would get it if he were from the same hostel, separated his work from Damini's comfort.

qa.q: What would have changed for the polytechnic candidate if Damini had followed that first gut feeling?
qa.a: He would probably have lost a job he was better at, just for speaking slowly and coming from a small polytechnic, and the workshop would have lost him.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague recalling the use of agreed criteria, the search for people from unfamiliar colleges, and the check of whether an outsider would be judged the same as someone from the same hostel.

The form closed at six. At 5:48 Alka still had two names on her screen for the single conference seat.
Naveen had grown up three streets from her in Indore. They spoke Malwi at lunch, and he'd covered for her the day her laptop died. Picking him would take ten seconds.
The other name belonged to someone from the Chennai office she had met only on video calls.
Alka opened the three criteria the team had written in January: work shipped this year, a talk proposal, and whether the person had presented before. She scored both honestly. The Chennai colleague had shipped more and had never been sent anywhere.
She stopped on one question. If the Chennai name were Naveen's, would I hesitate? No.
At 5:57 she submitted the form, then messaged Naveen before he heard it elsewhere: "Not this time. Next one, I'll push for you."

qa.q: When did the form close?
qa.a: The form closed at six, and Alka submitted it at 5:57.

qa.q: Why did picking Naveen feel so easy to Alka?
qa.a: Alka felt warm and grateful toward Naveen, who grew up three streets away and once covered for her, so choosing him felt natural and safe.

qa.q: Which check helped Alka decide fairly under time pressure?
qa.a: Scoring both names on the team's three written criteria and asking whether she would hesitate if the Chennai name were Naveen's kept friendship out of the choice.

qa.a: Naveen may feel disappointed, but also respected, because Alka told him directly and promised to push for him next time.

Mehak leaned on Zeenat's desk with two cups of cutting chai. "Put me on the Bandra site, na? We'll go together like college days."
